Predicting Daily City Service Complaints with Poisson & Negative Binomial Regression¶

NYC 311 Service Requests — Staten Island, 2021–2024 · Predictive Analytics Mini-Project¶

Problem. How many 311 service requests of each type will Staten Island receive on a given day, and which factors (complaint category, weekday, month, public holidays, long-term trend) are associated with higher complaint volumes?

Data. A subset of 311 Service Requests from 2020 to Present (NYC Open Data, dataset erm2-nwe9): all requests in Staten Island created 1 Jan 2021 – 31 Dec 2024, 12 columns (~106 MB, ~546k rows).

Why count models? The target (requests per day per category) is a non-negative whole number, so the natural models are Poisson regression and, when the counts are more variable than Poisson allows, Negative Binomial regression, both Generalized Linear Models (GLMs).

Syllabus module What is implemented
Introduction Definition & scope, descriptive vs predictive vs prescriptive, industry role, ethical considerations
Data Preparation & Exploration Data-collection challenges, type fixing, duplicates, text standardisation, missing values (incl. imputation), logical-error correction, outliers, EDA, feature engineering & selection
Logistic Regression & Inference (GLM part) Generalized linear regression, Poisson regression, overdispersion tests, Negative Binomial regression, coefficient inference (Wald, LR tests, IRRs)
Model Validation & Optimisation Chronological train-test split, time-based cross-validation, RMSE & MAE, grid search & random search, over-/under-fitting

Module 1 — Introduction¶

Predictive analytics uses historical data and statistical models to estimate future or unknown outcomes. Here: the number of 311 requests a city department will receive tomorrow, by category.

Importance & scope. 311 is New York City's non-emergency service line. Reliable daily forecasts let agencies (Sanitation, Police, Transportation, Housing, Parks) plan crews, call-centre staff and budgets. Scope of this project: daily request counts for 8 complaint categories in one borough, explained by calendar factors.

Analytics type Question In this project
Descriptive What happened? Cleaning report + EDA: volumes by category, weekday, month, year; response times
Predictive What will happen? Poisson & Negative Binomial models forecast daily counts for the unseen year 2024
Prescriptive What should we do? Convert the NB forecast into a "plan-for" capacity level (90th percentile) per category (§6)

Role in industries. Finance — counting claims/defaults per period; healthcare — hospital admissions or disease cases per week (classic Poisson/NB application); marketing — number of purchases or clicks per customer; IT — tickets or server errors per hour; government (this project) — service requests per day.

Ethical considerations.

  • The raw data contains request locations (latitude/longitude, ZIP) that can point to a household. The model uses only aggregated daily counts per category; coordinates are used only for data-quality repair and are never analysed per address.
  • Complaint volume reflects who reports, not only where problems exist: neighbourhoods with lower 311 usage may be under-served if resources follow predicted complaints blindly.
  • Models are interpretable GLMs, and their uncertainty is reported, so decisions remain transparent.

Module 2 — Data Preparation and Exploration¶

2.1 Data collection and its challenges¶

The data is collected operationally: residents report issues by phone, website (online), mobile app, and some records are created internally. Consequences for analysis:

  • Inconsistent text — complaint types are typed by different agencies (HEAT/HOT WATER vs Heat/Hot Water).
  • Missing values — e.g. no ZIP if the caller gave only a street, no closing date if the case is still open.
  • Logical errors — closing dates before creation dates, placeholder timestamps at exactly midnight.
  • Very long-running cases that distort response-time statistics.
  • Size — the full dataset has tens of millions of rows, so a relevant subset was exported via the NYC Open Data API (one borough, four years, 12 of 41 columns).

Consistency over time. Data collected over several years can change definition part-way through: types get renamed or move to other systems. A model trained on 2021–2023 would then make wrong forecasts for 2024. Every frequent type is therefore checked for years where it suddenly disappears:

Two kinds of problems appear:

Problem Types Correction
Renamed — the same complaint under a new name from 2022 Missed Collection (All Materials) → Missed Collection; Dirty Conditions → Dirty Condition merge into the current name
Not complaints / moved out of 311 — appointment bookings whose recording stopped Request Large Bulky Item Collection (stops 2023), Electronics Waste Appointment (stops 2024) remove: these are scheduling requests, not complaints, and keeping them would create a fake drop in 2023–24
Discontinued in 2021 only Sanitation Condition kept; it is small and is absorbed into the Sanitation category

NOT_COMPLAINTS = ["Request Large Bulky Item Collection", "Electronics Waste Appointment"]

Renamed types merged: 2 | appointment rows removed: 55,091 | rows remaining: 491,159 | distinct types: 208

Grouping the types into 8 categories. With 212 types, most of which are rare, a per-type model would be unstable. Types are grouped by meaning, using the responsible agency where it is unambiguous:

Category Rule
Noise type contains "noise"
Housing handled by HPD (heat, plumbing, mould, …)
Trees type contains the word "tree" (word match, so "street" is not caught)
Parking & Vehicles illegal parking, blocked driveway, abandoned/derelict vehicles
Sanitation handled by DSNY (missed collection, bulky items, dumping, …)
Water & Sewer handled by DEP (water system, sewer, lead, …)
Streets & Traffic handled by DOT (street condition, street lights, signals, …)
Other everything else
In [7]:
PARKING = {"illegal parking", "blocked driveway", "abandoned vehicle", "derelict vehicles", "derelict vehicle"}
def to_category(t, agency):
    t = t.lower()
    if "noise" in t: return "Noise"
    if agency == "HPD": return "Housing"
    if re.search(r"\btrees?\b", t): return "Trees"
    if t in PARKING or "vehicle" in t: return "Parking & Vehicles"
    if agency == "DSNY": return "Sanitation"
    if agency == "DEP": return "Water & Sewer"
    if agency == "DOT": return "Streets & Traffic"
    return "Other"
df["category"] = [to_category(t, a) for t, a in zip(df["complaint_type"], df["agency"])]
summary = df.groupby("category").agg(requests=("unique_key", "size"),
                                     example_types=("complaint_type", lambda s: ", ".join(s.value_counts().index[:3])))
summary.sort_values("requests", ascending=False)

2.4 Handling missing values¶

In [8]:
# (a) descriptor: free-text detail, not used by the model -> explicit "Unspecified" label
df["descriptor"] = df["descriptor"].fillna("Unspecified")

# (b) closed_date: is it missing because the case is still open?
cd_missing = df["closed_date"].isna()
display(pd.crosstab(cd_missing.map({True: "closed_date missing", False: "closed_date present"}), df["status"]))
status Assigned Closed In Progress Open Pending Started Unspecified
closed_date
closed_date missing 45 419 4717 361 1155 33 4
closed_date present 413 482996 19 329 576 2 90

Most missing closing dates belong to requests whose status is Open / In Progress / Pending / Assigned. These are legitimately missing because the case has not been closed yet, so they are kept as missing and not imputed. The model counts created requests, so this column does not affect the target.

In [9]:
# (c) incident_zip: impute from location where possible.
# Rows that have coordinates but no ZIP get the most common ZIP among complete rows in the same
# ~100 m grid cell (lat/lon rounded to 3 decimals) - a simple "nearest neighbours" imputation.
df["incident_zip"] = df["incident_zip"].str.strip()
valid_zip = df["incident_zip"].str.fullmatch(r"103(0[1-9]|1[0-4])")      # Staten Island ZIPs 10301-10314
print("ZIPs present but invalid:", (df["incident_zip"].notna() & ~valid_zip.fillna(False)).sum())
df.loc[~valid_zip.fillna(False), "incident_zip"] = np.nan

cell = df["latitude"].round(3).astype(str) + "," + df["longitude"].round(3).astype(str)
cell_zip = df[df["incident_zip"].notna() & df["latitude"].notna()].groupby(cell)["incident_zip"].agg(lambda s: s.mode().iloc[0])
need = df["incident_zip"].isna() & df["latitude"].notna()
before = df["incident_zip"].isna().sum()
df.loc[need, "incident_zip"] = cell[need].map(cell_zip)
after = df["incident_zip"].isna().sum()
print(f"Missing ZIPs: {before:,} -> {after:,}  (recovered {before - after:,} from coordinates)")
print(f"Rows still without ZIP or coordinates: {after:,} ({after/len(df):.2%}) - kept, ZIP is not a model input")

2.5 Correcting logical errors¶

In [10]:
df["response_hours"] = (df["closed_date"] - df["created_date"]).dt.total_seconds() / 3600

neg = df["response_hours"] < 0
print(f"Closed BEFORE created (impossible): {neg.sum():,} rows")
display(df.loc[neg, ["created_date", "closed_date", "complaint_type", "status"]].head(4))
# Correction: the closing timestamp is wrong, the request itself is real -> invalidate only closed_date
df.loc[neg, ["closed_date", "response_hours"]] = np.nan

midnight = df["created_date"].dt.strftime("%H:%M:%S").eq("00:00:00")
print(f"Created at exactly 00:00:00 (likely date-only placeholder): {midnight.sum():,} rows "
      "- the date is still valid, so the row is kept for daily counts")

closed_no_date = df["status"].eq("Closed") & df["closed_date"].isna()
print(f"Status 'Closed' but no closing date: {closed_no_date.sum():,} rows (inconsistent record, flagged)")
df["record_inconsistent"] = closed_no_date | neg

2.6 Outliers¶

(a) Response time. Response times are extremely right-skewed, so the IQR rule is applied on the log scale. A business rule is added: cases open for more than a year are also treated as long-running. Flagged requests are excluded from response-time statistics, but they remain valid requests for the daily counts, which only use the creation date.

(b) Daily volume. Days with unusually many requests are checked to decide whether they are data errors or real events.

In [11]:
lr = np.log1p(df["response_hours"].dropna())
q1, q3 = lr.quantile([.25, .75]); hi = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
print(f"Response-time upper IQR fence (log scale) = {np.expm1(hi)/24:,.0f} days")
df["slow_outlier"] = (np.log1p(df["response_hours"]) > hi) | (df["response_hours"] > 24 * 365)
print(f"Beyond the IQR fence: {(np.log1p(df['response_hours']) > hi).sum():,} | open more than 365 days: "
      f"{(df['response_hours'] > 24*365).sum():,} ({(df['response_hours'] > 24*365).mean():.1%}) -> both flagged as long-running")

daily_total = df.groupby(df["created_date"].dt.normalize()).size()
q1, q3 = daily_total.quantile([.25, .75]); fence = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
spikes = daily_total[daily_total > fence].sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f"\nDaily-volume upper fence = {fence:.0f} requests; days above it: {len(spikes)}")
top = df[df["created_date"].dt.normalize().isin(spikes.index[:6])]
display(top.groupby([top["created_date"].dt.date, "category"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
        .assign(total=lambda t: t.sum(1)).sort_values("total", ascending=False))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.4))
ax[0].hist(lr, bins=60, color=BLUE); ax[0].axvline(hi, color=ORANGE, lw=1.5, label="IQR fence")
ax[0].set_title("log(1 + response hours)"); ax[0].legend()
ax[1].boxplot(daily_total, vert=False, widths=.5, flierprops=dict(marker="o", markersize=3, markeredgecolor=MUTED),
              boxprops=dict(color=BLUE), medianprops=dict(color=ORANGE), whiskerprops=dict(color=BLUE), capprops=dict(color=BLUE))
ax[1].set_title("Requests per day (all categories)"); ax[1].set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Decision. The spike days are concentrated in single categories: a run of sanitation surges in late October 2021 (a collection backlog) and storm-related water/tree requests on 2 Sept 2021 (the remnants of Hurricane Ida). These are real events, not recording errors, so the raw records are kept. §2.10 shows how such one-off events are handled at the modelling stage so they are not mistaken for regular seasonality.

What the EDA shows.

  • Total volume changes from year to year, and not in the same direction for every category (see the yearly table below), so the model needs trend terms.
  • Weekday patterns differ by category: sanitation and housing requests drop sharply at weekends, while noise rises at weekends.
  • Seasonality differs by category: housing (heating) peaks in winter, trees and noise in summer.

These category-specific patterns motivate the interaction features in §2.9.

2.8 Building the modelling table: daily counts per category¶

Each row = one category on one day. All 1,461 days × 8 categories are included, so a day with no requests in a category appears explicitly as a 0. Leaving those days out would bias the counts upwards.

In [15]:
all_days = pd.date_range("2021-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="D")
cats = sorted(df["category"].unique())
counts = (df.groupby(["date", "category"]).size()
            .reindex(pd.MultiIndex.from_product([all_days, cats], names=["date", "category"]), fill_value=0)
            .rename("count").reset_index())
print(counts.shape, "| zero-count rows:", (counts["count"] == 0).sum())
counts.head()

2.9 Feature engineering¶

Feature Type Why
category categorical (8) different base volumes
dow categorical (7) weekly cycle seen in EDA
month categorical (12) seasonality
holiday binary US federal holidays (offices closed, fewer reports)
trend numeric (years since 1 Jan 2021) year-on-year decline
category × trend interaction categories trend differently (e.g. illegal parking rises while most others fall)
category × dow, category × month interactions each category has its own weekly and seasonal shape

Every category's variance is many times its mean. Poisson assumes variance = mean, so this is already a strong hint of overdispersion, which is tested formally in §3.2.

2.10 Train-test split (chronological)¶

Training: 2021–2023. Test: all of 2024, never used for fitting or model choice. A random split would let the model learn from days after the ones it is tested on.

Outlier treatment for modelling. A one-off event inside the training years, such as the October 2021 sanitation backlog found in §2.6, would otherwise be learned as "October is always a surge month" through the category × month feature. Category-days beyond the far-out fence (Q3 + 3·IQR, per category, training data only) are therefore removed from training. The test year is not touched, so the evaluation stays honest.

In [18]:
train = counts[counts["year"] <= 2023].copy()
test  = counts[counts["year"] == 2024].copy()

# Extreme one-off events: per-category "far out" fence Q3 + 3*IQR, computed on TRAINING data only.
q = train.groupby("category")["count"].quantile([.25, .75]).unstack()
far = train["category"].map(q[0.75] + 3 * (q[0.75] - q[0.25]))
extreme = train["count"] > far
display(train[extreme].groupby(["category", train.loc[extreme, "date"].dt.to_period("M")]).size()
        .rename("extreme days").reset_index().sort_values("extreme days", ascending=False).head(8))
train = train[~extreme].copy()
print(f"Extreme category-days removed from TRAINING: {extreme.sum()} of {len(extreme):,} ({extreme.mean():.2%}); "
      "the test year is left untouched")
print(f"train: {len(train):,} rows ({train.date.min().date()} to {train.date.max().date()})")
print(f"test : {len(test):,} rows ({test.date.min().date()} to {test.date.max().date()})")

2.11 Feature selection — likelihood-ratio (drop-in-deviance) tests¶

Each candidate term is removed in turn from the full model. If removing it significantly worsens the fit (LR test, p < 0.05) and raises AIC, it is kept. A Negative Binomial model is used for this test, with α fixed at a preliminary estimate, so that the p-values are not inflated by overdispersion.

In [19]:
FULL = "count ~ C(category) + C(dow) + C(month) + holiday + trend + C(category):trend + C(category):C(dow) + C(category):C(month)"
alpha0 = smf.negativebinomial("count ~ C(category) + C(dow) + C(month) + holiday + trend", train).fit(disp=0, maxiter=300).params["alpha"]
nb_fam = sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=alpha0)
full_fit = smf.glm(FULL, train, family=nb_fam).fit()
rows = []
for term, f in {"holiday": FULL.replace(" + holiday", ""),
                "category-specific trend": FULL.replace(" + C(category):trend", ""),
                "category x dow": FULL.replace(" + C(category):C(dow)", ""),
                "category x month": FULL.replace(" + C(category):C(month)", "")}.items():
    r = smf.glm(f, train, family=nb_fam).fit()
    lr_stat = 2 * (full_fit.llf - r.llf); df_ = full_fit.df_model - r.df_model
    rows.append({"term removed": term, "LR chi2": lr_stat, "df": int(df_), "p-value": stats.chi2.sf(lr_stat, df_),
                 "AIC without term": r.aic, "AIC full": full_fit.aic})
sel = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("term removed"); sel["keep?"] = sel["p-value"] < 0.05
sel

Module 3 — Generalized Linear Models: Poisson and Negative Binomial Regression¶

A GLM has three parts: (1) a probability distribution for $y$, (2) a linear predictor $\eta = x^\top\beta$, and (3) a link function $g(\mu) = \eta$.

Model Distribution Link Variance
Linear regression (Gaussian GLM) Normal identity: $\mu = \eta$ $\sigma^2$ (constant)
Poisson regression Poisson log: $\log\mu = \eta$ $\mu$
Negative Binomial (NB2) Negative Binomial log $\mu + \alpha\mu^2$

With the log link, $e^{\beta_j}$ is an Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR): the factor by which the expected count is multiplied when $x_j$ increases by one unit (or for a category versus its reference level). Coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood (iteratively re-weighted least squares).

3.1 Poisson regression¶

In [20]:
MAIN = "count ~ C(category) + C(dow) + C(month) + holiday + trend"
pois = smf.glm(MAIN, train, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()
print(f"Poisson (main effects): {int(pois.df_model)} parameters, log-likelihood = {pois.llf:,.0f}, AIC = {pois.aic:,.0f}")
pt = pd.DataFrame({"coef": pois.params, "std err": pois.bse, "z": pois.tvalues, "p": pois.pvalues, "IRR": np.exp(pois.params)})
pt.loc[["holiday", "trend", "C(dow)[T.Sat]", "C(dow)[T.Sun]"]]

3.2 Testing the Poisson assumption — overdispersion¶

  1. Pearson dispersion statistic $= \chi^2_{Pearson}/(n-p)$. It is ≈ 1 if Poisson is adequate.
  2. Cameron–Trivedi regression test of $H_0: \alpha = 0$ in $\text{Var}(y) = \mu + \alpha\mu^2$.
In [21]:
disp = pois.pearson_chi2 / pois.df_resid
mu = pois.mu; y = train["count"].values
ct = sm.OLS(((y - mu) ** 2 - y) / mu, mu).fit()
print(f"Pearson dispersion = {disp:.2f}   (1 = Poisson OK; >1 = overdispersed)")
print(f"Cameron–Trivedi: alpha_hat = {ct.params[0]:.3f}, t = {ct.tvalues[0]:.1f}, p = {ct.pvalues[0]:.1e}")

Pearson dispersion = 7.72   (1 = Poisson OK; >1 = overdispersed)
Cameron–Trivedi: alpha_hat = 0.138, t = 30.6, p = 1.6e-195

Both tests reject the Poisson assumption decisively. With overdispersion, a Poisson model's standard errors are too small: it reports effects as more certain than they are. The fix is a distribution with an extra variance parameter: the Negative Binomial.

3.3 Negative Binomial regression¶

The dispersion parameter $\alpha$ is estimated by maximum likelihood (statsmodels NegativeBinomial). It is then cross-checked by profile likelihood: refit the NB GLM over a grid of $\alpha$ values and pick the one with the highest log-likelihood.

In [22]:
nb_ml = smf.negativebinomial(MAIN, train).fit(disp=0, maxiter=300)
alpha_ml = nb_ml.params["alpha"]
grid = np.linspace(0.02, 0.30, 57)
prof = [smf.glm(MAIN, train, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=a)).fit().llf for a in grid]
alpha_prof = grid[int(np.argmax(prof))]
print(f"alpha (ML) = {alpha_ml:.4f} | alpha (profile likelihood) = {alpha_prof:.4f}")

nb = smf.glm(MAIN, train, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=alpha_ml)).fit()

# Likelihood-ratio test Poisson (alpha = 0) vs NB. alpha=0 is on the boundary -> p-value halved (chi-bar-squared)
lr_stat = 2 * (nb.llf - pois.llf)
print(f"LR test Poisson vs NB: chi2 = {lr_stat:,.0f}, p = {0.5 * stats.chi2.sf(lr_stat, 1):.1e}")
cmp = pd.DataFrame({"log-likelihood": [pois.llf, nb.llf], "AIC": [pois.aic, nb.aic],
                    "Pearson dispersion": [disp, nb.pearson_chi2 / nb.df_resid]}, index=["Poisson", "Negative Binomial"])
display(cmp)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.plot(grid, prof, color=BLUE); ax.axvline(alpha_ml, color=ORANGE, lw=1.5, label=f"ML alpha = {alpha_ml:.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel("alpha"); ax.set_title("Profile log-likelihood of alpha"); ax.legend(); plt.show()

alpha (ML) = 0.1714 | alpha (profile likelihood) = 0.1700
LR test Poisson vs NB: chi2 = 35,455, p = 0.0e+00
log-likelihood AIC Pearson dispersion

Negative Binomial -36,382.662 72,819.325 1.124

The NB model has a far lower AIC, its dispersion statistic is close to 1, and its standard errors are several times larger than Poisson's. They are larger because they are honest: Poisson was over-confident.

3.4 Final model: Negative Binomial with category-specific weekly and seasonal patterns¶

The terms selected in §2.11 are added as interactions. $\alpha$ is re-estimated for this specification by profile likelihood.

In [24]:
prof_full = [smf.glm(FULL, train, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=a)).fit().llf for a in grid]
alpha_full = grid[int(np.argmax(prof_full))]
nb_full = smf.glm(FULL, train, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=alpha_full)).fit()
pois_full = smf.glm(FULL, train, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()
print(f"alpha (full model) = {alpha_full:.4f}  - smaller than before: interactions explain part of the extra variation")
models_aic = pd.DataFrame({"parameters": [pois.df_model + 1, nb.df_model + 2, pois_full.df_model + 1, nb_full.df_model + 2],
                           "AIC": [pois.aic, nb.aic, pois_full.aic, nb_full.aic]},
                          index=["Poisson - main effects", "NB - main effects", "Poisson - with interactions", "NB - with interactions"])

Module 5 — Model Validation and Optimisation¶

5.1 Cross-validation on the training years (expanding window)¶

Fold Train Validate
1 Jan 2021 – Jun 2022 Jul – Dec 2022
2 Jan 2021 – Dec 2022 Jan – Jun 2023
3 Jan 2021 – Jun 2023 Jul – Dec 2023

Each fold trains on at least 18 months, so every month appears in training and the category trends are estimated from more than one year.

Metrics. RMSE (penalises large misses) and MAE (average absolute miss, in requests per day). For hyperparameter tuning, the mean NB log-likelihood on the validation year is also used, because it judges the whole predicted distribution, not just the mean.

In [27]:
FOLDS = [("2022-07-01", "2023-01-01"), ("2023-01-01", "2023-07-01"), ("2023-07-01", "2024-01-01")]
def nb_loglik(y, mu, a):
    return stats.nbinom.logpmf(y, 1 / a, 1 / (1 + a * mu)).mean()

def cv_score(formula, family_name="nb", alpha=None):
    out = []
    for start, end in FOLDS:
        tr, va = train[train.date < start], train[(train.date >= start) & (train.date < end)]
        fam = sm.families.Poisson() if family_name == "poisson" else sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=alpha)
        m = smf.glm(formula, tr, family=fam).fit()
        mu_tr, mu_va = m.predict(tr), m.predict(va)
        a = alpha if alpha else 0.05
        out.append({"train RMSE": rmse(tr["count"], mu_tr), "val RMSE": rmse(va["count"], mu_va), "val MAE": mae(va["count"], mu_va),
                    "train loglik": nb_loglik(tr["count"], mu_tr, a), "val loglik": nb_loglik(va["count"], mu_va, a)})
    return pd.DataFrame(out).mean()

print("CV, NB main-effects model:"); display(cv_score(MAIN, alpha=alpha_ml).to_frame("mean over folds").T)

CV, NB main-effects model:
train RMSE val RMSE val MAE train loglik val loglik
mean over folds 16.935 17.883 13.807 -4.188 -4.247

5.2 Hyperparameter tuning — Grid search and Random search for α¶

$\alpha$ controls how much extra variance the NB model allows. Above, it was estimated by maximum likelihood on all training data. Here it is treated as a hyperparameter and tuned for out-of-sample predictive log-likelihood with the time-based CV folds:

  • Grid search — evaluate 15 evenly spaced values.
  • Random search — evaluate 15 values drawn at random (log-uniform).
In [28]:
def cv_alpha(a): return cv_score(FULL, alpha=a)["val loglik"]
grid_a = np.linspace(0.02, 0.50, 15)
grid_res = pd.Series([cv_alpha(a) for a in grid_a], index=grid_a)
rand_a = np.sort(np.exp(RNG.uniform(np.log(0.02), np.log(0.50), 15)))
rand_res = pd.Series([cv_alpha(a) for a in rand_a], index=rand_a)

tuning = pd.DataFrame({
    "best alpha": [grid_res.idxmax(), rand_res.idxmax(), alpha_full],
    "CV mean log-likelihood": [grid_res.max(), rand_res.max(), cv_alpha(alpha_full)],
    "evaluations": [len(grid_a), len(rand_a), "-"]}, index=["Grid search", "Random search", "ML / profile estimate"])
display(tuning)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))
ax.plot(grid_res.index, grid_res.values, "o-", color=BLUE, ms=5, label="grid search")
ax.plot(rand_res.index, rand_res.values, "o", color=ORANGE, ms=6, label="random search")
ax.set_xlabel("alpha"); ax.set_ylabel("validation mean log-lik"); ax.set_title("Tuning the NB dispersion parameter"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
best alpha CV mean log-likelihood evaluations
Grid search 0.123 -4.036 15
Random search 0.159 -4.051 15
ML / profile estimate 0.080 -4.058 -

Grid search and random search reach almost the same optimum. Random search gets there without testing every grid point, which is its advantage when there are several hyperparameters. The CV-tuned α is somewhat larger than the in-sample ML estimate: future periods are more variable than the training data suggests, because of shifts between half-years. A larger α widens the prediction intervals, which is the safer choice for planning.

5.3 Over-fitting and under-fitting — model-complexity ladder¶

Models from too simple to very complex, compared on training vs validation error (same CV folds):

In [29]:
ladder = {
    "1. intercept only": "count ~ 1",
    "2. category only": "count ~ C(category)",
    "3. main effects": MAIN,
    "4. + category trend, x dow, x month (chosen)": FULL,
    "5. + category x dow x month (3-way)": FULL + " + C(category):C(dow):C(month)",
}
lad = pd.DataFrame({k: cv_score(f, alpha=alpha_full) for k, f in ladder.items()}).T
lad["n params"] = [len(smf.glm(f, train, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit().params) for f in ladder.values()]
display(lad[["n params", "train RMSE", "val RMSE", "val MAE", "train loglik", "val loglik"]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
x = np.arange(len(lad))
ax.plot(x, lad["train loglik"], "o-", color=BLUE, ms=6, label="training (mean log-likelihood)")
ax.plot(x, lad["val loglik"], "o-", color=ORANGE, ms=6, label="validation (mean log-likelihood)")
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels([k.split(".")[0] for k in lad.index]); ax.set_xlabel("model (see table)")
ax.set_ylabel("higher = better"); ax.set_title("Under-fitting (left) vs over-fitting (right)"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
n params train RMSE val RMSE val MAE train loglik val loglik
1. intercept only 1 21.224 20.503 16.822 -4.861 -4.781
2. category only 8 17.825 18.076 13.859 -4.429 -4.495
3. main effects 27 16.898 17.815 13.737 -4.291 -4.398
4. + category trend, x dow, x month (chosen) 153 12.817 14.938 11.178 -3.898 -4.058
5. + category x dow x month (3-way) 681 12.015 15.428 11.599 -3.835 -4.111

Reading the ladder. Model choice uses the validation log-likelihood (it judges the whole predicted distribution) and MAE. RMSE is also shown, but it swings with a few extreme days, such as a sanitation surge in one validation half-year.

  • Models 1–3 under-fit. Their training and validation log-likelihoods are the lowest, because they ignore that every category has its own weekly, seasonal and trend pattern.
  • Model 4 (chosen) has the best validation log-likelihood and the lowest validation MAE.
  • Model 5 over-fits. It adds over 500 extra parameters, so its training fit improves further while its validation log-likelihood and MAE get worse. That growing train–validation gap is the signature of over-fitting.

5.4 Final evaluation on the unseen test year (2024)¶

The models are refitted on all of 2021–2023 and evaluated once on 2024. A simple baseline is included: "the average for this category and weekday in the training data."

Poisson - main effects 20.758 13.936 0.000
Negative Binomial - main effects 20.749 13.930 0.000
Poisson - with interactions 17.894 11.068 0.000
Negative Binomial - with interactions (final) 18.002 11.189 0.000

Result on 2024.

  • Both interaction models clearly beat the baseline and the main-effects models. Category-specific patterns are what drive accuracy.
  • Poisson and NB give almost identical point forecasts, because they share the same log-linear mean. The NB model is still preferred: its AIC is far lower, its standard errors are honest, and its prediction intervals are calibrated (§6). Poisson's intervals would be far too narrow.
  • Linear regression (Gaussian GLM) with the same features comes close on average error, but it is the wrong model for counts. It can produce negative predictions (see the last column), its effects are additive rather than multiplicative, and it assumes the same variance for a 5-request day as for a 100-request day, so its uncertainty statements are invalid.

6. From prediction to decision (prescriptive analytics)¶

The NB model gives a full probability distribution for each day's count, not only the mean. A department that wants enough capacity on 90% of days should plan for the 90th percentile of NB($\mu$, $\alpha$). The table checks how often that level actually covered 2024 demand.

In [32]:
size = 1 / alpha_full
test["plan_90"] = stats.nbinom.ppf(0.90, size, size / (size + test["pred"]))
cover = test.groupby("category").apply(lambda g: pd.Series({
    "avg forecast/day": g["pred"].mean(), "avg plan-for level (90%)": g["plan_90"].mean(),
    "days covered in 2024": (g["count"] <= g["plan_90"]).mean() * 100}))
print(f"Overall coverage of the 90% plan-for level in 2024: {(test['count'] <= test['plan_90']).mean():.1%}")
cover.round(1)

* Cleaned 546,250 raw requests (491,159 complaints kept): standardised 224 complaint-type spellings into 208 types and 8 categories, recovered 68 missing ZIPs from coordinates, invalidated 536 impossible closing dates.
* Overdispersion: Poisson dispersion = 7.7 (should be ~1); NB alpha = 0.080.
* AIC: Poisson 81,920 vs Negative Binomial 68,039 (lower is better).
* Holidays change expected requests by -24%; fastest-rising category: Housing (+14.1%/yr), fastest-falling: Streets & Traffic (-13.5%/yr).
* Best test-year model by RMSE: Poisson - with interactions (RMSE 17.89, MAE 11.07); baseline RMSE 19.91.
* The NB 90% plan-for level covered 89% of 2024 category-days.

Key takeaways

  1. Data preparation — real public data needed type fixing, case standardisation, category grouping, imputation, logical-error correction and outlier review before it could be modelled.
  2. Poisson vs Negative Binomial — daily complaint counts are strongly overdispersed. Poisson gives the same kind of mean predictions but badly understates uncertainty; Negative Binomial fixes this, with far lower AIC and calibrated prediction intervals.
  3. Drivers of complaint volume — the complaint category, the weekly cycle (different for each category), seasonality (winter heating vs summer trees and noise), public holidays and a declining long-term trend.
  4. Validation — a chronological split, time-based CV and the complexity ladder show that the chosen model generalises to a full unseen year without over-fitting.

Limitations. Weather (storms, heat waves) is not included, but it drives the largest spikes. Category trends are extrapolated linearly (on the log scale), so a category whose growth stops, as Housing did in 2024, will be over-predicted. Complaint counts measure reporting, not the true incidence of problems. The analysis covers one borough only.
